diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let's assume that the statement is true for $n-1$ rows and fix the matrix
Therefore, by the inductive hypothesis matrix $\hat{C}$ satisfies the equality criteria from the Proposition \ref{pr} and hence contains three rows satisfying Lemma \ref{le}.
Taking one of the other two submatrices to be the new matrix $\tilde{C}$ we break point (iii) and hence establish the validity of the strict version of the desired inequality.

issues.failure_explanation: The inductive hypothesis (Proposition \ref{pr} for $n-1$ rows) only yields that $\hat C$ has $\max\sigma_2 = 1/\sqrt{n-1}$ and the three-group structure; it says nothing about which $2\times2$ submatrices attain $1/\sqrt{n-1}$. Read literally the assertion is false whenever a group has more than one row: all $pq+pr+qr$ pairs from different groups (not three) have $\sigma_2 = 1/\sqrt{n-1}$. The step is load-bearing, because the replacement $\tilde C$ must still satisfy condition (ii) $\sigma_2(\tilde C)=1/\sqrt{n-1}$ while violating (iii). The inclusive statement actually needed (each of the three cross submatrices attains $1/\sqrt{n-1}$) is true but is neither stated nor proved here.

failure_location.quote: These three rows form the three $2 \times 2$ submatrices of $\hat{C}$ with the smallest singular value equal to $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the sentence by the inclusive statement and justify it, e.g. by applying the equality-case block analysis carried out later in the paper to $\hat C$: cross-block entries of $M$ vanish, i.e. $\delta_{ij}=2/(n-1)$, so $\sigma_2^2=1/(n-1)$ for every pair of rows from different groups.
issues.overall_effect: The strict inequality claimed in Case A, and with it the 'only if' half of the equality criteria in Proposition \ref{pr} and Corollary \ref{co}, are not established by the argument as written.
issues.title: Case A strictness step uses an unproved (and literally false) count of the extremal submatrices
issues.why_classification: The claim actually needed is recovered by a short local argument already contained in the paper's equality-case analysis; restating the sentence and supplying it preserves every claim and guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Applying the similar considerations to all pairs of $w$'s and taking into account (\ref{ws}), we get $|u| = |v| = \frac{1}{2n} + \frac{1}{2p}$ and $(u, v) = |u||v|$, which finalizes the proof of the equality criteria.

issues.failure_explanation: The argument selects two vectors inside a block and extracts pairwise lower bounds $|u|+|v|\ge 1/n+1/p$, which are then summed with $\sum|w_i|=2$. For a block of size 1 no pair exists and nothing is obtained; for a block of size 2 the summing pins only $|u|+|v|=1/n+1/p$, not the two magnitudes separately. Both cases occur in genuine equality configurations (e.g. $n=4$ with $p=2,q=r=1$), so the necessity half of the equality criteria is unproved there. The claimed values follow instead from the diagonal entries of (\ref{blck}), i.e. from the first displayed identity taken with $u=v$.

failure_location.quote: Let us select from $w_1, \ldots, w_n$ two vectors corresponding to the first block of (\ref{blck}) and denote them by $u$ and $v$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Apply the displayed identity $(u, v) - (|u| - \frac{2}{n})(|v| - \frac{2}{n}) + \frac{2}{n^2} = \frac{2}{pn}$ to the pair $(u,u)$ — its diagonal entry in (\ref{blck}) — which gives $|u| = \frac{1}{2n} + \frac{1}{2p}$ for every vector of the block, singleton blocks included; the pairwise identity then gives $(u,v)=|u||v|$.
issues.overall_effect: The magnitude part of the equality criteria in Proposition \ref{pr} (and of the characterization (2) in Corollary \ref{co}) is unestablished for groups of one or two rows, hence for most small $n$.
issues.title: Derivation of the equality magnitudes fails for blocks of one or two vectors
issues.why_classification: A one-line use of the already displayed block identity fills the gap for every block size and preserves all claims and guarantees.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The corresponding equality is achieved if and only if the rows of the matrix are clustered into three non-empty groups of $p, \, q, \, r > 0$ pairwise collinear vectors, with the squared magnitudes equal to $\frac{1}{2n} + \frac{1}{2p}$, $\frac{1}{2n} + \frac{1}{2q}$ and $\frac{1}{2n} + \frac{1}{2r}$, respectively.
Now let us analyze the equality case. In terms of matrix $M$, it can be achieved only if $M$ is non-negative (but not positive).

issues.failure_explanation: The whole equality-case analysis derives the three-group configuration from the assumption that equality holds ('it can be achieved only if $M$ is non-negative'), i.e. it proves only the necessity half of the stated biconditional. Nothing shows that a matrix with orthonormal columns whose rows form three groups of pairwise collinear vectors with squared magnitudes $\frac{1}{2n}+\frac{1}{2p}$, $\frac{1}{2n}+\frac{1}{2q}$, $\frac{1}{2n}+\frac{1}{2r}$ actually attains $\max_{i\ne j}(|w_i|+|w_j|-|w_i+w_j|)=2/n$: this needs a computation of the cross-group and within-group quantities using the closure relation $px+qy+rz=0$.

failure_location.quote: which finalizes the proof of the equality criteria.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Supply the missing converse: with $x,y,z$ the three row-squares and $px+qy+rz=0$, compute $(x,y)=(c^2-a^2-b^2)/(2pq)$ for $a=|px|,b=|y|q,c=|rz|$ and verify that every cross-group pair has $M_{ij}=0$, i.e. $\delta_{ij}=2/n$, while within a group $M_{uu}=2/(pn)>0$ gives $\delta<2/n$; hence $\max\delta=2/n$.
issues.overall_effect: One half of the biconditional in Proposition \ref{pr}, and correspondingly of the equality characterization (2) in Corollary \ref{co}, is unsupported; the sufficiency of the advertised equality criterion is not established anywhere in the paper.
issues.title: The 'if' direction of the equality criteria is never proved
issues.why_classification: The converse is true and follows from a contained computation with the paper's own identities, so no new architecture or loss of scope is needed; but a genuine argument (not routine algebra) must be added to support half of the headline biconditional.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $v_1, v_2, v_3 \in \mathds{R}^2$ be vectors with pairwise non-collinear squares. Then the three $2 \times 2$ matrices composed of these vectors as rows have pairwise different first (and second) right-singular vectors.
Thus, the conjugated square of the first right-singular vector is oriented as the sum of the squares of vectors $v_i$ and $v_j$.

issues.failure_explanation: The inference that pairwise non-collinear vectors $v_1^2,v_2^2,v_3^2$ have pairwise non-collinear sums is false. Counterexample: $v_1=(1,0)$, $v_2=(1/\sqrt2,1/\sqrt2)$, $v_3=(\sqrt\varphi,1/\sqrt\varphi)$ with $\varphi=(1+\sqrt5)/2$ have squares $(1,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,2)$ (pairwise non-collinear), yet $v_1^2+v_2^2=(1,1)$ and $v_1^2+v_3^2=(2,2)$ are collinear. By the paper's own formula the first right-singular vector of the matrix with rows $v_i,v_j$ is oriented as $v_i^2+v_j^2$, so the matrices with rows $(v_1,v_2)$ and $(v_1,v_3)$ have the same first (and second) right-singular vector up to sign — both $(1,\sqrt2-1)^T$ — contradicting the lemma's statement.

failure_location.quote: Since $v_1^2$, $v_2^2$ and $v_3^2$ are pairwise non-collinear, their sums $v_1^2 + v_2^2$, $v_1^2 + v_3^2$ and $v_2^2 + v_3^2$ are pairwise non-collinear too, which finalizes the proof of the lemma.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the lemma by the weaker statement actually needed and prove it: the three sums $v_1^2+v_2^2$, $v_1^2+v_3^2$, $v_2^2+v_3^2$ cannot all be pairwise collinear (all three collinear would force one of the determinants $\det(v_i^2,v_j^2)$ to vanish), so at most two of the three cross submatrices share a given right-singular vector line, which is enough to pick a $\tilde C$ breaking condition (iii).
issues.overall_effect: Lemma \ref{le} is used in Case A ('By Lemma \ref{le} vector $(\pm 1, 0)^T$ can be a right-singular vector of at most one of these three submatrices') to force a strict inequality; with the lemma false that step is unsupported, so the strictness in Case A and hence the 'only if' direction of the equality criteria in Proposition \ref{pr} and Corollary \ref{co} are unreliable.
issues.title: Lemma \ref{le} is false: sums of pairwise non-collinear squares need not be pairwise non-collinear
issues.why_classification: The lemma as stated is false and must be weakened and reproved, which is more than a local edit, but a short determinant argument supplies exactly what the Case A step needs, so all claims of Proposition \ref{pr} and Corollary \ref{co} survive with no new proof architecture.
